newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Right-wing S.Africans condemn universities bill.
newsitem.headline: Right-wing S.Africans condemn universities bill.

text.p: South Africa's cabinet on Wednesday approved new "equitable" university legislation but the youth wing of a white separatist party condemned it as the death knell for Afrikaans-language campuses and an incitement to a race war.

Education Minister Sibusisu Bengu told a news conference after the cabinet decision that the Higher Education Bill would establish "a single, coordinated system of higher education while encouraging diversity".
"It will achieve an equitable framework for the funding of the higher education system and the efficient utilisation of resources," he said.
Bengu said he was urging all universities, including the five which in the past catered mainly for Afrikaans-speaking whites, to adjust to the needs of black students who preferred English.

He singled out the University of Stellenbosch -- a cultural icon for South Africa's Afrikaner community -- as one that could be required under the bill to meet constitutional guidelines on accommodating all official languages.
"At Stellenbosch University...English is used for a few courses that are offered beyond the first degree level but no English is used at all for undergraduate work," the minister said.
He cited the example of Zulu students who struggled with their courses at Stellenbosch because of language difficulties.

"For them to spend five years just because the university has not accommodated them in studies that should take four years is costly for the government... The frustration is brought over to the entire system," Bengu said.
Many of South Africa's leading Afrikaner intellectuals, businessmen and politicians studied at Stellenbosch.

The youth wing of the right-wing Freedom Front, representing Afrikaners who want self-rule to protect their cultural identity, said in a statement the bill would indirectly abolish Afrikaans campuses.

"Funds will be allocated as a reward to universities which educate members of so-called disadvantaged communities, forcing Afrikaans universities to change their demographic composition in order to survive financially," the party said in a statement.

"It is an insensitive step which we will oppose in every possible way and which promises to be a major accelerator on the road to future ethnic conflict in this country," it said, adding that the bill reflected an attitude of revenge rather than reconiliation.
The Freedom Front won less than two percent of the vote in South Africa's 1994 all-race election.
